title: Uniform Circular Motion
subcategory: Laws of Motion / Motion in a Plane — Circular Motion

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 11 — Motion in a Plane / Laws of Motion

summary: In uniform circular motion, speed stays constant but velocity direction keeps changing, requiring a constant centre-seeking (centripetal) acceleration v²/r supplied by a real, identifiable force.
explanation: Even though speed is constant in uniform circular motion, velocity is not — its direction is continuously changing — so there must be an acceleration, directed towards the centre, called centripetal acceleration ac = v²/r = ω²r. Centripetal FORCE is not a new, separate kind of force; it is simply the name given to whatever real force (tension in a string, gravity for orbiting satellites, friction for a car turning, the normal reaction's horizontal component for a banked road) happens to supply this centre-directed acceleration, Fc = mv²/r. For a car on a level road, friction alone provides this force, limiting the safe turning speed; banking the road (tilting it at angle θ so tanθ = v²/rg) lets the horizontal component of the normal force contribute too, allowing higher safe speeds even with less reliance on friction. Angular velocity ω (rad/s) relates to linear speed by v = ωr, and time period T = 2π/ω = 2πr/v. 'Centrifugal force' — the outward force felt by an observer inside the rotating frame — is a pseudo-force that only appears in the non-inertial (rotating) reference frame; from outside (inertial frame), the object only ever experiences the real, inward centripetal force.
commonMisconceptions: Believing centripetal force is an additional force alongside gravity/tension/friction — it is only a label for the net inward component that those real forces already provide.
Confusing centripetal force (real, inward, in an inertial frame) with centrifugal force (a pseudo-force that appears only in the rotating/non-inertial frame).
Forgetting that speed constant does not mean acceleration is zero in circular motion — direction change alone produces acceleration.
examples: A stone whirled in a horizontal circle on a string: tension in the string supplies the centripetal force.
Banked race-track curves let cars turn safely at higher speeds than a flat road allows for the same friction.
genZNote: Circular motion out here changing direction every second while insisting 'my speed never changed.'
